I want to build an HTPC (or go with a SFF prebuilt, haven't decided yet). If it is always on, and the OS is running on an SSD - what kind of R/W is happening when nothing is going on (no user apps, nothing running - like when nobody is using it)? Is it a bad idea to leave a pc on all the time if it has an SSD?
Question about always-on PC and SSDs

iotop shows the disk activity in real time. You need to install it from the repository as it is not normally included. Works like htop.

In theory there shouldn't be anything happening on an idle system but there are a few usual suspects (like journalling) that keep gnawing IO unless disabled. iotop helps finding those out.

When it comes to SSDs there are a few additional thing to be considered. Choice of file system, partition alignment, TRIM support, etc. Read here for the full picture.

In a well configured system running a PC with SSD shouldn't hurt at all.
iotop shows basically nothing, a dozen bytes or kb here and there. Would I be correct in assuming such miniscule r/w would be an issue?

Essentially, yes. Unlike a mechanical HDD that will overwrite the same spot when changing file contents, the firmware of an SSD will make sure that each successive write targets a new block. Think of it sort of like a round-robin writing routine -- if you were to write a couple KB to the same file over and over, the drive would "sequentially" (even though that really doesn't apply to solid state) write through all the blocks before it came back to the original block again. So you're not going to wear out any particular chunk of the drive faster than any other; or at least that's the idea.

If you're really concerned about it, though, you can isolate specific, high-traffic volumes like /tmp and /var/tmp, and mount them as tmpfs in fstab. This will create ram disks for them, removing the need to write data to your drive at all. Make sure you understand the limitations of tmpfs before you do this: namely space limitations and volatility of data. But for tmp directories this is usually pretty safe; all my machines run in this config.
